subtitle: When hiring through Connect 700, you will prepare a job-related demonstration, coordinate access and base decisions on the work a qualified participant can do.
scope: For supervisors and hiring managers considering Minnesota’s Connect 700 pathway. Follow current MMB, HR, and statutory requirements. This course supplements understanding and does not replace the annual training required by Minnesota Statutes section 43A.15, subdivision 14. It does not determine program eligibility, make accommodation decisions, or authorize appointments.
introTranscript: Connect 700 offers an alternative way for qualified applicants with disabilities to demonstrate job abilities. Managers need to understand the pathway and prepare work that actually reveals the position’s essential functions. This course follows a practice analyst role from recruitment through a supported demonstration and an appropriate decision. It separates eligibility, qualifications, access, performance evidence, and formal authority. Disability is not a reason to lower an unrelated standard or to impose a new one; the question is whether the person can perform the job with or without reasonable accommodation through the authorized process.

intro.heading: Understand what the pathway is for
intro.body:
Standard interviews and tests may not allow some qualified applicants with disabilities to show their abilities. MMB describes Connect 700 as an alternative pathway with a pre-probationary on-the-job demonstration of up to 700 hours. Eligibility and minimum qualifications are separate requirements handled through the authorized process.

A manager does not decide eligibility from appearance, a diagnosis they infer, or a personal conversation. Use the program’s proof and HR direction. Likewise, a certificate does not by itself establish the qualifications for every position.

Current law and authorized instructions govern the actual process. Older guides may not reflect every statutory change. Before recruitment or a demonstration, confirm the applicable procedures and complete required employer training. This learning course is not a substitute for that requirement.

items.title: Eligibility
items.body: Eligibility for Connect 700 and qualification for a particular position answer different questions. Certification establishes access to the pathway under its rules; it does not establish every job requirement. In a practice analyst vacancy, HR first confirms the applicable pathway and qualifications rather than assuming a certificate guarantees appointment.

items.title: Qualification
items.body: The pathway gives a qualified applicant an alternative way to demonstrate ability to perform essential functions. This connects evaluation to the work instead of relying only on a conventional assessment. A useful demonstration therefore produces relevant evidence, such as accurate analysis and a clear explanation, with reasonable accommodation as needed.

items.title: Authority
items.body: Use current MMB guidance, applicable requirements, and the responsible offices for operational decisions. A manager should not interpret disability eligibility independently or create a local version of the pathway. Course learning supports understanding but does not replace required training or the formal responsibilities of HR and other authorized offices.

tabs.label: Standard method
tabs.body: A standard assessment can collect useful evidence, but its format may not provide every qualified applicant an effective opportunity to demonstrate ability. Consider what it actually measures. A fast oral test, for example, may poorly represent a job that principally involves careful written analysis.

tabs.label: Alternative
tabs.body: An alternative demonstration focuses on ability to perform the essential work within the authorized pathway. Its value depends on relevant tasks, clear expectations, and access. It is a structured opportunity to demonstrate ability, not a promise that qualification requirements disappear.

tabs.label: Shortcut
tabs.body: A shortcut would treat a certificate, diagnosis, or course completion as sufficient evidence for a job decision. That looks administratively simple but confuses separate requirements. Confirm eligibility, qualifications, and demonstrated ability through the proper process instead.

check.question: Which approach correctly distinguishes the requirements?
check.correct: Program eligibility, job qualifications, and evidence from the demonstration.
wrong: Treat a certificate as automatic appointment.
Treat a diagnosis as proof of job ability.
Treat this course as a substitute for required annual training.
check.feedbackCorrect: The pathway has different decisions with different evidence and authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A certificate does not guarantee appointment or establish every qualification. A diagnosis does not tell you what a person can demonstrate, and this course does not replace formal required training. Keep eligibility, qualifications, and evidence of essential functions distinct.

intro.heading: Prepare work that demonstrates essential functions
intro.body:
A demonstration should reveal whether the person can perform the essential work. Start with the position and confirm its functions through the proper process. Choose tasks that give a reasonable opportunity to show those functions, not puzzles or style preferences unrelated to the role.

For a practice analyst, a task might involve interpreting a small dataset, checking a conclusion, and explaining its limits. Speed in a rapid oral exchange may not be the relevant measure if the job requires careful written analysis. Do not add a new condition because the pathway makes someone unfamiliar to the team.

Explain the expected work, tools, support, and feedback. Coordinate accommodations through the responsible process and preserve actual standards for essential functions. A fair demonstration requires both job-related expectations and a usable opportunity to meet them.

lessons.keyStatement: Use real work and clear expectations rather than another hidden interview.

items.title: Function
items.body: Choose work that reflects essential functions rather than an unrelated preference. In a practice analyst demonstration, interpreting a small dataset and explaining its limits may be relevant. A surprise memory puzzle is not useful simply because it creates a score; the task must connect to the actual job.

items.title: Expectation
items.body: Explain the task, standards, tools, and feedback process before evaluating the result. An applicant who knows what accuracy means can direct effort toward the work. If the job normally permits reference materials, an unexplained ban can introduce a different demand that needs review rather than better evidence.

items.title: Opportunity
items.body: Coordinate the conditions needed for a fair opportunity to demonstrate work. Relevant standards and appropriate access can coexist. For example, HR can help confirm the use of an accessible spreadsheet while the evaluator continues to examine the accuracy and reasoning required for the analyst position.

tabs.label: Relevant
tabs.body: A relevant task produces evidence that can be connected directly to the job. It may take more preparation than a generic exercise, but makes feedback and the final decision easier to explain. Document the essential function and the evidence the task is intended to reveal.

tabs.label: Unrelated
tabs.body: An unrelated test can appear objective because everyone receives the same puzzle or time limit. Equal format does not establish job relevance. It may measure comfort with the test rather than the essential function, leaving the evaluator with precise but unhelpful results.

tabs.label: Clear
tabs.body: Clear expectations reduce avoidable confusion and support meaningful evaluation. They do not guarantee a successful result or remove standards. They let the evaluator distinguish the quality of the work from a misunderstanding of an instruction that was never explained.

check.question: Which task best fits the analyst demonstration?
check.correct: A real analysis task with clear job-related expectations and coordinated support.
wrong: A task judged by criteria disclosed afterward.
check.feedbackCorrect: It measures the actual function through an understandable opportunity.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A puzzle, a surprise social exercise, or a criterion added later may seem useful because it separates applicants. The problem is that separation alone does not show job ability. Use relevant work, clear expectations, and coordinated support to collect interpretable evidence.

intro.heading: Coordinate access from application through work
intro.body:
A participant cannot demonstrate a task if instructions, tools, or communication are unusable. Current statutory provisions address accommodations during application, hiring, and the demonstration. Coordinate requests promptly through the responsible process; a manager should not diagnose the person or decide an exception alone.

In the analyst example, an inaccessible spreadsheet or unclear onboarding may prevent the work sample from reflecting ability. Record the barrier separately from the performance question and arrange the appropriate response. Do not simply lower expectations or conclude the person cannot do the work.

Keep medical information within authorized processes. The supervisor needs enough functional information to support work, not a public account of the person’s condition. Ask HR and accommodation staff how to proceed when a barrier affects the demonstration or its timing.

lessons.keyStatement: Do not assess ability through an avoidable access failure.

items.title: Barrier
items.body: An access barrier and a performance concern are different observations. If an applicant cannot use an inaccessible file, that establishes a problem with the work conditions, not inability to analyze its contents. In a practice review, repair the access issue before interpreting the missing analysis as job evidence.

items.title: Coordination
items.body: Current requirements provide for timely reasonable accommodation across the applicable stages. Coordinate requests through the responsible process rather than waiting until a final decision. For example, clarify the functional need and the available work format early so the demonstration can examine the intended essential function.

items.title: Privacy
items.body: Share only information needed for the authorized purpose. A team may need to know that a document must be accessible without receiving the applicant’s diagnosis. Keeping the discussion functional protects privacy and directs attention to what needs to change for the work to proceed.

tabs.label: Access problem
tabs.body: An access problem describes a condition that prevents an effective opportunity to do the task. Repairing it improves the evidence available to the evaluator. It does not predetermine whether the resulting work meets the essential function; that question remains for the actual demonstration.

tabs.label: Performance question
tabs.body: A performance question concerns the relevant work after appropriate conditions and expectations are considered. It can lead to specific feedback or a documented evaluation. Do not use that label to bypass an unresolved tool or communication barrier that could explain the result.

tabs.label: Unsupported inference
tabs.body: An unsupported inference turns an access problem into a judgment about disability or ability. It may feel like an explanation, but adds information the evaluator does not have. Record the observed condition, coordinate the repair, and examine the resulting work.

check.question: How should a failed inaccessible task be interpreted?
check.correct: Identify and address the access barrier before drawing an unsupported ability conclusion.
wrong: Treat it as automatic proof of inability.
Ask the team to discuss the person’s diagnosis.
check.feedbackCorrect: A barrier can distort the evidence; support and standards both require the proper process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An inaccessible tool is not evidence of inability. Sharing a diagnosis does not make the file usable, and ignoring essential functions does not produce a sound demonstration either. Coordinate access first, then examine the relevant work under appropriate conditions.

items.text: The file format cannot be used with arranged tools.
Instructions are unavailable in a usable form.

A supported work product meets the criterion.
Medical documentation belongs in the authorized process.
A diagnosis should not be shared at the team meeting.

intro.heading: Give feedback tied to observed work
intro.body:
A demonstration needs timely, concrete feedback. “You are not a good fit” gives neither a criterion nor a path to understand the concern. Describe the task, expected result, observed result, and next step through the current authorized documentation process.

For the analyst, feedback might identify a calculation checked incorrectly or a limitation omitted from a report. State what occurred without attributing it to disability or comparing personality with another employee. Include strengths as well as gaps.

Check whether instructions, opportunity to learn, and support were provided. A missing tool is not the same as a repeated error after usable instruction. Keep the record factual, protect information, and use current HR and MMB guidance for required check-ins and forms rather than improvising a timetable from memory.

Distinguish observed performance from an inference about disability.

What should happen?
lessons.keyStatement: Feedback should help a person understand the work, not guess the supervisor’s meaning.

items.title: Observation
items.body: Feedback should identify the observed work and the criterion it addresses. For example, explain that a calculation was accurate but the report did not identify a major limitation. This gives the applicant something concrete to respond to, unlike a general statement that the person does not fit.

items.title: Support
items.body: Consider whether unclear instructions, unavailable tools, or unresolved access affected the result. These conditions may change how the evidence should be interpreted. They do not require inventing success; they require distinguishing what the applicant demonstrated from what the process failed to make possible.

items.title: Next step
items.body: Agree on the next step through the authorized process. A clarified instruction, an accessible format, or a further relevant task may be appropriate. Use current feedback and evaluation requirements from the responsible offices rather than relying on a remembered timetable from an older guide.

tabs.label: Vague
tabs.body: Vague feedback is quick to deliver but difficult to act on. A statement such as “not a good fit” does not identify the essential function or evidence. It can conceal personal preference and leaves both the applicant and the person screening unable to evaluate the reasoning.

tabs.label: Specific
tabs.body: Specific feedback connects an observation, a standard, and a next step. It can recognize what worked while identifying what needs attention. This supports learning and a reviewable decision without promising that every concern will be resolved or that appointment is assured.

tabs.label: Inference
tabs.body: A disability-based inference substitutes a presumed explanation for the work evidence. Even when offered as concern, it can distract from actual conditions and requirements. Describe what happened and ask the authorized process to resolve relevant support or evaluation questions.

check.question: Which feedback is useful?
check.correct: A specific observed result against a stated expectation, with a clear next step.
wrong: A surprise criterion introduced after the task.
check.feedbackCorrect: The person and the screener can understand what happened and what is expected.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personality impressions, diagnosis-based explanations, and new criteria may seem to explain a difficult result. They do not identify the essential function or what the work showed. Give specific feedback, check relevant support conditions, and use the authorized evaluation process.

items.text: A stated limitation was omitted.
The calculation matches the task criterion.
The required tool was unavailable.
The instruction was not provided.
The person cannot succeed because of a guessed diagnosis.

intro.heading: Use evidence and authority for appointment decisions
intro.body:
The demonstration is a route to assess actual ability, not a requirement to keep a person waiting until every possible hour is used. Current statute addresses conversion when the person demonstrates the essential functions with or without reasonable accommodation. Work with HR and MMB on the authorized decision and documentation.

Summarize job-related evidence, feedback, opportunity, and support. If a concern remains, do not invent termination, extension, or appointment rules. Older rule or guide language should be checked against amended statute and current instructions.

Tell the participant what is happening through the proper process without guaranteeing an outcome controlled by another authority. Formal grievance and other rights remain available through their responsible routes. The course does not authorize an appointment or adverse action.

lessons.keyStatement: Up to 700 hours is a limit, not a reason to postpone a justified decision.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: The current statutory pathway permits a demonstration of up to 700 hours; elapsed hours alone are not the measure of ability. In a practice case where essential functions have been demonstrated earlier, the manager should consult HR about the applicable conversion requirements rather than assuming every applicant must wait for the full limit.

items.title: Authority
items.body: Appointment decisions require the relevant evidence and the authorized process. Managers should not invent local conversion, extension, or termination rules. A clear summary identifies the essential functions demonstrated, the evidence, relevant accommodation, and the question that HR or MMB must confirm.

items.title: Rights
items.body: Preserve the formal protections and routes that apply to the pathway. A course summary cannot replace current requirements or resolve a grievance. If a disagreement arises, provide accurate information about the responsible process without promising a result or discouraging the person from using it.

tabs.label: Hours-only
tabs.body: An hours-only approach is easy to track but can mistake a time limit for a required waiting period or an automatic appointment rule. Time is part of the pathway’s structure. It does not substitute for evidence of essential functions and the applicable conversion requirements.

tabs.label: Evidence-based
tabs.body: An evidence-based approach connects the work demonstrated to the essential functions and brings the decision to the responsible offices. It is more demanding than checking a clock, but makes the basis for action understandable and avoids treating time as the only condition.

tabs.label: Improvised
tabs.body: An improvised rule may appear to solve a local problem quickly, yet can contradict the authorized pathway. When older guidance and a current requirement appear different, describe the conflict and seek clarification. Do not create a convenient local rule to bridge the gap.

check.question: What should guide a conversion question?
check.correct: Demonstrated essential-function ability and current authorized requirements with HR and MMB.
check.feedbackCorrect: The decision belongs to the evidence and governing process, not an arbitrary waiting period.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The phrase “up to 700 hours” does not make hours alone the decision rule. Inventing a local requirement or promising appointment before authorized review creates a different problem. Document demonstrated ability and confirm the applicable next step with HR or MMB.

intro.heading: Support the next stage and review the pathway
intro.body:
After an authorized conversion, the employee still needs usable onboarding, clear supervision, development opportunities, and the appropriate accommodation process. Do not treat the person as a permanent demonstration project or disclose their history to justify ordinary support.

Review the pathway’s operation with HR and program partners: Were expectations clear? Were access arrangements timely? Was feedback useful? Did decisions use current requirements? Use appropriate process evidence and protect individual records. A single experience does not establish success or failure for everyone.

If a barrier is found, assign a concrete repair and next review. Required program reporting and training remain with their authorized processes. The practical learning here helps managers ask better questions and prepare better work; it is not certification of compliance or a substitute for formal responsibilities.

items.title: Transition
items.body: After conversion, support the employee’s ordinary transition into supervision, development, and participation. Do not continue an informal permanent trial label. In a team in this example, the employee should receive relevant development opportunities rather than being excluded because colleagues still describe the person as a demonstration participant.

items.title: Review
items.body: Review the pathway by examining process conditions: instructions, access, feedback, evidence, and decisions. Keep personnel and medical information in appropriate protected records. A single case may reveal a repair worth making, but does not establish that every participant had the same experience.

items.title: Improve
items.body: Choose a process improvement with a responsible person and a follow-up date. For example, clarify how accessible work materials are prepared before the next demonstration. Formal reporting and required training have their own responsibilities; a local improvement report should not claim to satisfy all of them.

tabs.label: Person label
tabs.body: A continuing person label can make the pathway seem like a permanent status. It risks shaping assignments and expectations after its actual purpose has ended. Discuss the employee’s current role, work, and support needs instead of preserving an informal trial category.

tabs.label: Employment
tabs.body: An employment view recognizes the transition to the ordinary workplace and its development opportunities. It still permits relevant supervision and feedback. The difference is that the employee’s continuing experience is not framed as indefinite participation in the earlier demonstration.

tabs.label: Process learning
tabs.body: Process learning asks what the organization can improve from the experience. It can strengthen future access without exposing personal details. Keep conclusions proportional: one successful conversion is encouraging, but does not establish universal compliance or remove the need for ongoing review.

check.question: What is a sound pathway review?
check.correct: Examine expectations, support, feedback, and decision steps with appropriate partners and privacy.
wrong: Publish medical details to show success.
Declare all duties met because one person converted.
Keep treating the employee as a trial after conversion.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review improves the pathway while respecting ordinary employment and formal duties.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Publishing medical details does not improve the pathway. A conversion also does not prove every requirement was met, and a permanent trial label misunderstands the transition. Review the process, protect individual information, and support the employee’s current role and development.
